nodes.text: THREE SERMONS OF SAINT AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN.
FIRST SERMON.
ON THE PERFECT [MAN].

I. The heavenly command of our Lord Jesus Christ [is plain], and leaves nothing uncertain or tangled in obscurity: in it, with open truth, the selling off of possessions is enjoined, and the paying out of the price is not passed over in silence. "Sell," he says, "all that you possess, and give alms." Those occupied with heavenly duties he does not allow to be entangled in the care and trouble of worldly possession; and those already near to God by the very profession of devotion, or rather joined to Christ by sincerity of mind, he frees from the care and anxiety of worldly possession. Every course of your work and every motion of your thought he snatches from the world, [you] whom he has deigned to assign to heaven. For from this comes what he openly commands: "Do not take thought, saying, What shall we eat, or what shall we wear? (Matth. vi, 31) And do not take thought for tomorrow" (Ibid., 34). So that what he had commanded could easily be fulfilled, with all anxieties of thought removed, "Sell," he says, "all that you possess, and give alms." He has cut away every excuse of cunning greed, he who bids [us] leave nothing to take thought for tomorrow, who has commanded that the whole amount of [our] substance be paid out.

II. But let us take up again what was set out before, for the discussion to be examined: "Do not take thought," he says, "saying, What shall we eat, or what shall we wear? For the nations seek these things. But your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things" (Ibid. 32). Thought born of distrust destroys in you the faith of [your] divine profession; and while you fear that something may be lacking for the next day, you must needs doubt the promises; then you draw back your hands from just works; and so it comes about that, held back by weak thought, you desist from good work, and in desisting from good work you lose the name of religion and of God, and, compared by the very faithlessness of your weakness to the unbelieving heathen, you incur the detestable name of unbelief and the label of pagan folly. For it belongs to Christians to think on the future with most faithful hope, and to gentiles in despairing faithlessness to seek the present, as Christ says: "Do not take thought, saying, What shall we eat, or what shall we wear? For the gentiles seek these things." And he added: "But your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things."

III. The divine word has reminded [us] that knowledge of our condition of need cannot be hidden from the heavenly Father, and it commands that all things be supplied to us by his providence and care, if, as we cling to works of justice and are held by the search for the heavenly kingdom, no anxiety over present hardships pricks us; for it says: "Seek first the kingdom of God and his justice, and all things will be added to you" (Ibid. 33). Those devoted to the duties of justice and piety, and occupied with heavenly exercises, he makes safe about all things, and secure: so that you are not called away from knowledge of the Father, are not drawn away from recognition of the Only-begotten, nor desist from the gift and profession of the Holy Spirit; [that] you do not stray from meditation on the command, nor from hope in the promise, nor from faith in what is believed, nor from love of neighbour, nor from the perfection of the commandment, about which Moses (Deut. vi, 6, 8) warns that it should always sit in our heart, always be present before our sight, bound by meditation to all our members, always cling to our senses. Of this David [says]: "Your justifications will always be songs to me, Lord" (Ps. cxviii, 54). And again: "In the law of the Lord was his will, and in his law he will meditate day and night" (Ps. i, 2). And elsewhere it is written: "Let the book of this law not depart from your hand; and you shall meditate on it day and night" (Jos. i, 8). Likewise the Apostle exhorts and warns, writing to Timothy: "Meditate on these things, be in them, so that your progress may be manifest to all" (I Tim. iv, 15).

IV. The will of a religious man, held by heavenly laws and occupied day and night with meditations on divine justification, has no empty time in which to think of the world, to look after property, to embellish country estates, to cultivate the art of farming, to reckon up revenues, to examine expenses. For if it seizes on this, it abandons that, according to what the Lord's word declared: "No one who puts his hand to the plough (that is, to heavenly work and the sign of the Lord's cross) and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God" (Luke ix, 62). For one cannot carry out both, which are hostile to each other in principle, different in truth, and rivals in will. For this one thinks of the world, that one longs for heaven; this one presses on with worldly accounts, that one gives itself to divine prayers and meditations. Finally, to prove my words by facts and confirm the assertion of my speech by deeds, I will use an example. If, while you hold a divine book in your hands, and your eyes are taking in the letters as you read, and you are committing the divine precepts to your mind, an account book or the deeds of a purchased property should happen to be handed to you, you must needs put down the book of the divine law which you were holding in your hands, in order to take the documents of worldly accounts to read through; and so it comes about that, preferring worldly accounts to divine books, you become a despiser of the precept by which it is enjoined with frequent warnings that the book should not be absent from the hands, that meditation on it should not rest in the heart. And therefore the Lord in the Gospel, wishing to provide for the perfect and the complete, decreed that all they possessed should be sold and paid out, so that by no reckoning could they be torn away from love of him or called away from meditation [on him]. Hence it is that he forbade [us] to take thought even for the very necessities of mortals, that is, clothing, food and drink, and promised that all things would be supplied by him to those who fulfil everything; so that, as has often been said already, you may be held back by no necessity from the business of the divine work; so that no barrenness of the year may disturb you; no lack of crops and dryness of the fields, nor failing yields of olives and vines torment you; no losses of dying cattle shake you.

V. Let devotion remain free and unshaken, so that, possessed by love of him and of the Lord Christ, it may resound with hymns, give itself to prayers, persist in fasts and vigils, and fittingly and aptly break out into that prophetic song: "The fig tree will not bear fruit, there will be no growth in the vines. The work of the olive will fail; the fields will not yield food. The sheep will fail from the pasture, and there will be no oxen in the stalls. But I will exult in the Lord, and rejoice in God my saviour" (Hab. iii, 17, 18). He always rejoices and is glad in the Lord who, having thrown off the burdens of worldly possession, or rather paid them out for the needs of the brethren, is touched by neither impending nor present blows. The exaction of tribute does not press on him with necessity, nor the fields of a property lying neglected, nor orchards disfigured by the desertion of their tillers; savage slaughter by hail does not trouble him, nor plenty of rain held back by a long drought, nor the frequent devastation of storms; the collapse of houses does not torment him, nor anxiety over the condition of sick and dying neighbours, nor the flight of slaves, nor theft.

VI. All things that have been transferred to heaven are in safety: they are disturbed by no false charge, assailed by no lawsuit, lost by no worldly damage, which have been sent ahead to heaven, which are kept with God as guardian, as the Lord Jesus Christ says: "Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy, and where thieves dig through and steal. But store up treasure for yourselves in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys, and where thieves do not dig through and steal. For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also" (Matth. vi, 19, 20, 21). Following the example of this precept, the apostle Paul warns the most blessed Timothy that the rich of this world must be instructed not to be lifted up by worldly pomp, but to attain the loftiness of Christian humility; and not to be deceived by the perishing hope of worldly riches, but to be enriched by the everlasting gifts of the divine promises. "Command the rich of this world," he says, "not to be high-minded, nor to hope in the uncertainty of their riches, but in the living God, who provides us with all things in abundance to enjoy; to do good, to be rich in good works, to give readily, to share, to lay up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may lay hold of true life" (I Tim. vi, 17-19).
SERMON II.
Against those who say that property should not be sold off, but that mercy should be done from its produce.

I. The saving command of Jesus Christ is: "Sell all that you possess, and give alms" (Luke xii, 33). The faithfulness of the Lord as teacher is plain, for he not only ordered [property] to be sold off, but also directed what should be done with what was sold. But this faith perverse teachers darken with trifling and frivolous words; whom the apostle Paul condemned in advance as adulterers, not of the flesh, but, what is worse, of the divine words, saying: "Adulterating the word of God" (II Cor. ii, 17). And again: "Do you not know that whoever corrupts the temple of God, God will destroy him?" (I Cor. iii, 17). And [there is] that which Christ recalled in the gospel, rebuking the Pharisees, saying: "You reject the commandments of God in order to establish your own traditions" (Mark vii, 9).

II. "Property," they say, "is not to be sold off, but kept; and works of mercy are to be performed from its revenues." Why do you cover, under the garment of a work of mercy, the burning greed for having and keeping property? Why do you shade the outrage of your impiety under the veil of piety? Why do you snatch from believers, by subtle persuasion, the Lord's command, illustrious in its very purity? Why, by feigned and pretended talk, do you deny the heavenly commandment to religious people? Why, with a serpent's counsel, do you shut paradise to the servants of God, you who, not entering yourself, also hide the keys of the heavenly kingdom from those who wish to enter? You are not wiser or greater than Christ, who ordered [this] to be done; not better than the apostle Paul, who carried it out. He, as soon as he was enlightened by grace, did not yield to flesh and blood in fearful sufferings; he did not go up to Jerusalem to obtain counsel from the Apostles who had gone before him, since divine and heavenly converse had instructed him in all the proclamations of the faith; he did not make for Cilicia, his own city, to receive the paternal inheritance which he had abandoned to the poor for Christ; he did not even defend the nobility of the Roman stock from which he drew the origin of his blood, knowing it to have been disgraced by the Lord's passion; but [went] through the region of Arabia, so that he might bring to all mortals, by faithful proclamation, [the news] that that venerable name, which he had persecuted with injury, which he had attacked with eloquence and with the envy of the Pharisees, was saving and divine. Who then is proved like Paul in deeds, Paul endowed with manifold triumphs? He who strips himself of all the chains and pomps of the world, and will rightly be called a servant of God; who, despite envious detractors, perseveres in fulfilling the precepts of the Lord Christ, who said: "Sell all that you possess, and give alms (Luke xii, 33); and behold, all things are clean for you" (Ibid. xi, 41).

III. In the precept the selling off is enjoined, and the distribution of what is sold is required. To the devoted, purification of mind is promised; for those cleansed of filth the heavenly kingdom is prepared. I ask, what more do you seek, or what is left, except that, if the servants do not do what is commanded, God should do what he threatens? He also said: "If you have not been faithful in the unjust mammon, who will give you what is true? And if you have not been faithful in what is another's, who will entrust to you what is yours?" (Ibid. xvi, 11, 12). "And these will go into eternal burning, but the just into eternal life" (Matth. xxv, 46).
SERMON III.
ON CHARITY.
From the [teaching] of St Paul the apostle against the wicked, who envy the good.

I. Now that the gifts of perfection have been gone through and examined, let us proceed, as we promised, to the weightier and more eminent proclamations of the Apostle; who declared that neither knowledge of mystery, nor loftiness of eloquence, nor the generous kindness of mercy, nor the sublime merit of faith, nor the strong and fearless constancy of martyrdom can profit, if brotherly charity, and that sincere, is lacking. For what does it profit to feed at your expense one whom you kill with the sword? Or what does it help to cherish with any nourishment whatever one whom you pursue with the hatred of a robber? He lacks all the duties of kindness who, inflamed with the flames of hatred, persecutes in his brother the grace either conferred by divine aid, or acquired by the labours of fasting, or by assiduity in prayer, or by persistence in vigils and by every kind of virtue. For charity without mercy is imperfect, because mercy is a member of the body of charity; on the other hand, mercy without charity is nothing, because every member dies which has been torn away or cut off from the whole body. For charity is a kind of summit of all the members, holding the citadel, joined and bound into which all the duties of the virtues endure; without which the reward of all good things either languishes or perishes, as the Apostle says: "If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but have not charity, I am like sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal. And if I have prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so that I move mountains, but have not charity, I am nothing. And if I give away all my means, and distribute all I have to the poor, and if I hand over my body to be burned, so that I may glory, but have not charity, it profits me nothing" (I Cor. xiii, 1-3).

II. Charity is the mother of all good things, the beginning of mercy, the origin of kindness, the fount of benevolence, the head of justice, the fulfilment of the law, the perfection of the precepts. Without this one thing all things either collapse weakened or lack a kingdom. For even to have prophetic insight is nothing; and to know mysteries is a light thing; it is little to put demons to flight; and to accomplish every kind of virtue, if charity is lacking, is empty. Hence the Lord Christ says thus: "Many say to me on that day: Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name do great works of power? Then I will say to them: Depart from me, I do not know you, you who work iniquity" (Matth. vii, 22, 23). It is a work of iniquity to wish a man to be preferred to a man, for brother to envy brother, for one not to wish for another what he wishes for himself; and, though we have one natural condition, to wish to set one condition above another.

III. When the author of our salvation, conscious of the nature proper to divinity, showed himself mortal to all mortals, and presented himself a man to all men, and, what is greater, subjected [his] condition to [our] condition, he fitted the form of his body to the form of our body, so that by this sacrament he might make loftiness equal to humility and humility to loftiness; and so that in this he might fulfil the Father's will, he who said: "I did not come down from heaven to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me" (John vi, 38). And again: "The Son of man," he says, "did not come to be served, but to serve" (Matth. xx, 28). And readily he, setting aside the loftiness of majesty, took the form of a slave, as the Apostle says: "Who, though he was in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a slave" (Philip. ii, 6, 7). And that [saying]: "Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, enters the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven" (Matth. vii, 21).

IV. But we cannot do the will of the Father unless we first know what that will is. The will of God, then, on the authority of the apostle Paul, is "our sanctification" (Thess. iv, 3); us whom he has cleansed from every stain of the ancient contagion through the regeneration of the saving bath, by this our profession, by which we believe that God came in the weakness of the flesh, by which we confess him born of a virgin, by which we do not deny that he was subjected to [our] condition, by which we extol Christ crucified, proclaim him buried, and raised by the glory of God. Hence, since we see that so much of his sanctification has been conferred on us from the profession alone, from this we can understand how great a reward can be conferred from imitating him and from his will being known and carried out; about which the Apostle teaches us thus: "that you may know what is the will of God, what is good, and pleasing, and perfect" (Rom. xii, 2). The will of God, brother, is love of neighbour: that you rejoice with your brother, that you do not envy one better, that you prefer an inferior to yourself, that you do not commit an offence, that you forgive one committed, that you outdo in honour those who honour [you], that you anticipate in love those who love [you], that you pray for enemies, that you feed adversaries, that you do not hate persecutors (Rom. xii, 9 ff.). Thus every virtue becomes an honour and an ornament: faith, perfection, mercy, martyrdom, a body burned by flames; thus we become sons of God, when we resemble the heavenly Father in works (Rom. viii, 16, 17); thus we are joined to Christ by right of inheritance, when we bestow good things on the good and the wicked, when we either forget an injury or forgive from the heart one held on to, when with more eminent love we spend not only our goods but ourselves for friends; thus we shall abound in the Holy Spirit, whose we also are, if with all gentleness we fulfil the things that belong to kindness.

V. Hence the Lord Christ admonished the Apostles as they hastened to take vengeance on the inhospitable Samaritans, saying: "Do you not know whose spirit you are?" (Luke ix, 55) — of gentleness, surely: who is a stranger to all agitations, who is shaken by no injury, who is at peace from all disturbances, who, resting on tranquillity, is mild, kind, gentle and pleasant; whom Elijah saw in the third place, as Scripture says: "You will go out tomorrow, and stand before the face of the Lord; and behold, the Lord will pass by, and behold, a great and mighty wind, breaking mountains and shattering rocks before the face of the Lord: and the Lord [was] not in that wind; and after the wind an earthquake: and the Lord [was] not in the earthquake; and after the earthquake a fire: and the Lord [was] not in the fire; and after the fire the voice of a gentle breeze: and in it [was] the Lord" (III Kings xix, 11, 12). But what Elijah was found worthy to see through a sacrament, the prophet Isaiah openly learned by the Lord's revelation: "Upon whom," he says, "shall I rest, except upon the humble, and the gentle, and the one who trembles at my words?" (Isai. lxvi, 2). So too that Samuel, Samuel the illustrious priest, by the Lord's command rejected and set aside the most distinguished brothers, alike in appearance, equal in stature, not unequal in valour, and by the Lord's command anointed as king David their brother, lowly in humility, weak in gentleness, and milder in spirit of tranquillity; hence he himself prayed and said: "Remember, Lord, David, and all his mildness" (Ps. cxxxi, 1). This choice of God has always remained and remains: that he opposes and casts down the proud, and cherishes and raises up the humble. This exaltation cannot be without humiliation, nor election without rejection, nor calling without discrimination. And therefore, when the weak and despised and last are loved, the highest and great are rejected; for to God great things are weak, and weak things are great. The apostle Paul taught this, who showed that the calling of believers descends from this election: "See your calling, brothers," he says, "for not many are wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble; but God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong; and God chose the ignoble and contemptible things of this world, the things which are not (contemptible, that is), to destroy the things which are (contemptible, namely): so that no flesh may glory in his sight" (I Cor. i, 26-29).

VI. So let those glory in the world who glory in the flesh; let those glory in the flesh who glory in man, who are lifted up by the honours of the world, who are puffed up by riches, who are proud of nobility. "But far be it from us to glory, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we ourselves are crucified to the world, and the world is crucified to us" (Gal. vi, 14); whose pomps and pleasures we lost and cast away already then, when with a better course we made the passage to heaven; just as the admonition of John, teacher of the heavenly life, set out for us the form and image of living: "Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the charity of the Father is not in him: for all that is in the world is the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the ambition of the age; which is not from the Father, but from the lust of the age" (I John ii, 15, 16).

VII. He who hates the world does not dread the hatred of the world: for he himself by his own hatred provoked the world to hatred of him; and therefore it is not right either to dread or to shudder at its hatred, if it strives to weigh out to you what it has proved you paid out to it. So this worldly hatred, by whose detractions we are torn, by whose blasphemies we are mocked, is neither new nor sudden; for we know well that it was long ago brought against the Lord Christ and his apostles, as the Evangelist says: "If they called the father of the household Beelzebub, how much more his household?" (Matth. x, 25). And: "If the world hates you, know that it hated me first" (John xv, 18). So too the Apostle says: "We have been made a spectacle to this world, and to angels, and to men" (I Cor. iv, 9); that is, to the gentiles and to false brothers, who under the name of religion transform themselves into angels of light. Indeed he openly covered this above and below. "Already," he says, "you are filled, you have become [rich]: without us you reign; and would that you did reign, so that we too might reign with you" (Ibid., 8). And below: "We are fools for Christ's sake, but you are prudent in Christ; we are weak, but you are strong. To this very hour we both hunger and are naked, and are buffeted, and are unsettled (that is, we do not resist, or do not defend [ourselves]), and we labour, working with our own hands: we are cursed, and we bless; we suffer persecution, and we endure; blasphemed, we entreat: we have become like the refuse of this world, the offscouring of all" (Ibid., 10-13). This is the apostolic teaching, this the mystery of God and of Christ, this the heavenly way of life, this the spiritual profession; this the world does not receive; this hypocrisy rejects, as the Apostle says: "The natural man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God: for it is foolishness to him" (I Cor. ii, 14).

VIII. Now the fruits of the Spirit are those which the Apostle enumerates, saying: "Charity, joy, peace, patience, goodness, gentleness, faith, mildness, continence, chastity" (Gal. v, 22, 23). And that about which the same Apostle warned the Church of the Ephesians in his letter: "Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption" (Ephes. iv, 30). The Spirit is grieved by contrary desires, that is, by the works of the flesh, which among other hidden ones are these: "Enmities, contentions, rivalries, indignations, provocations, angers, quarrels, dissensions, sects, envies, drunkenness, revellings (that is, gluttons)" (Gal. v, 20, 21). For by these works the Spirit is grieved, offended; it deserts and departs, as Solomon says: "For the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit" (Wisd. i, 5).

IX. "Do not," says the apostle Paul, "grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption" (Ephes. iv, 30). The day of redemption is the day on which, redeemed by the saving gift of pardon, we are freed from the sentence of death; on which we put off the old man with his deeds, and put on the new, who is created according to God in good works. For on that day we are also sealed to the Holy Spirit, when we are made complete by all the sacraments, as the Evangelist says: "And when Jesus had been baptised, he at once came up from the water; and behold, the heavens were opened, and he saw the Spirit of God descending from heaven like a dove, coming upon him" (Matth. iii, 16). The dove is simple in innocence, or innocent in simplicity, not violent in clamour, not [...] in cruelty, not irascible in temper, not hostile with the bitterness of gall. And therefore, once that same Spirit had been received, which descended in its likeness, the Apostle added, saying: "Let all bitterness, and anger, and indignation, and clamour, and blasphemy be taken away from you" (Ephes. iv, 31). Bitterness is to conceive enmities, to belch out hatreds, to vomit forth poisons, to disparage one's neighbours, to spread deadly things abroad, as it is written in Deuteronomy: "Our enemies are senseless. Their vine is from the vine of Sodom, and their branches from Gomorrah; their grape is a grape of gall, and their cluster one of bitterness. Their wine is the rage of dragons, and the incurable fury of asps" (Deut. xxxii, 31, 32, 33). And David: "Their throat is an open sepulchre, with their tongues they acted deceitfully, whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness" (Psal. xiii, 3). Anger, he says: anger is to envy the better man, to detract from the fortunate, to groan at a neighbour's progress; whence the Prophet speaks thus: "The sinner will see, and will be angry, he will gnash with his teeth, and will waste away" (Psal. cxi, 10). Indignation, he says: indignation is to take it ill that an inferior is made equal to a superior in the gift of grace, or set before him in rank of charism; whereas the Apostle says to the Galatians: "There is neither slave nor free; there is neither male nor female; but you are all one in Christ Jesus" (Gal. iii, 28).

X. The most blessed Paul teaches in almost all his letters that those called to the faith out of every nation, rank, nobility, age or sex have been made one in Christ; by the sacrament of whose passion the princedom of the world was dishonoured, nobility disfigured, loftiness laid low, lowliness exalted, the exalted brought down, the filthy purified, the fallen raised up, and the dead brought to life. So in Isaiah (Isa. xl, 4) the hollows of the valleys are filled, the heights of the mountains are brought low; so crooked things are made straight, and rough places levelled; so the slopes of all the hills, balanced into evenness, are brought down into the flatness of the plains; so the cedars of Lebanon are thinned, and the shoots of the saplings, strengthened, grow fat; so the fierceness of lions, made tame, is joined to oxen, and, disdaining the fat of flesh, feeds on straw with the ox; so the wolf, its rage laid aside, grazes the meadows of the plains with the lambs; so the bear agrees with the calf, and the kid with the leopard (Ibid. xi, 6, 7); so infants thrust their hands into the holes of asps, and they do no harm; so the variety of the human race, since it does not belong to God by [its] good, will be brought back into one; so diversity of birth agrees in unity; so rival conditions are made equal, while through baptism they die to their worldly birth, and through grace are born to the nobility of heaven, as the prophet Isaiah says: "Behold now the ruler, the Lord of Sabaoth, will throw the glorious into confusion with might, and those who are proud will be crushed with disgrace, and will be humbled, and the lofty will fall by the sword. And Lebanon will fall with its high ones" (Ibid. x, 33, 34). The divine word often compares Mount Lebanon and the tops of its cedars to the worldly kingdom and its princes; which kingdom and its ministers the Lord Christ cast down and crushed by his passion. And so that the diversity of the passages should not trouble us, the same prophet, pointing to the person of the Lord Christ himself, who was to accomplish all these things, went on to say: "A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise up from its root" (Ibid. xi, 1). The root certainly signified the person of David, from whose seed Christ was born in the flesh, who, springing from the loins of his father Jesse, extended [his] lineage to the flower of the Lord's birth in the flesh. Then he added, saying: "The Spirit of God shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and kindness; the spirit of the holy fear of God shall fill him" (Ibid., 2, 3). And to show more openly that Christ must be understood, he continues, saying: "He shall not judge according to glory, nor reprove according to eloquence; but he shall judge with humble judgement, and shall reprove the glorious of the earth, and shall strike the earth with the word of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he shall slay the wicked" (Ibid., 4); that is, with that word and breathing of the lips with which he said: "The princedom of this world (that is, the dominion) shall be cast out" (John xii, 31). Of which again: "The princedom of the world comes, and will find nothing in me" (John xiv, 30). And to show the sacrament of the cross, he added, saying: "And he shall be girded with justice about the loins, and wrapped with truth about the sides" (Isai. xi, 5). "Then," he says (that is, from that time), "the wolf shall graze with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid, and the calf, and the bull, and the lion shall graze together; and a little child shall lead them" (that is, a priest, either innocent through smallness of age, or supported by the purity of innocence, shall govern them). "And the ox and the bear shall graze together" (and their nation shall be one), "and the lion and the ox shall eat straw" (that is, dry food) (Ibid., 6, 7). And lest my interpretation be judged presumptuous or rash by careful hearers, I will insert among my interpretations the discussion of the apostle Paul, who says: "Strip yourselves of the old man with his deeds, and put on the new, who is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created him. Where there is not male and female, Greek and Jew, circumcision and uncircumcision, barbarian and Scythian, slave and free: but Christ is all and in all" (Coloss. iii, 9, 10, 11). Those stripped of the deeds of the old [man] he clothes with the way of life of the new man, who is Christ; nor did he allow them to be left unclothed, but covered them with the garment of an honourable way of life and the brightness of good works. "Put on," he says, "as the elect of God and holy, the bowels of mercy, kindliness, humility, patience, modesty, bearing with one another, and forgiving one another, if anyone has a complaint against another; as the Lord also forgave you, so do you also" (Ibid., 12, 13).

XI. By God's gift all things have been forgiven us; we shall remain unharmed if we too forgive the offences of our brothers; if we are joined by the bonds of charity in an inseparable knot (Ibid., 14 ff.); if by the gift of peace we rejoice in mutual love; if we build ourselves up with the divine words; if we rouse [one another] to heavenly things with psalms; if we invite [one another] to things above with hymns; if all that we do in deed, that we speak in word, that we embrace in thought, we accomplish in the fear of God; giving thanks to the Father through the Son, praising God in Christ, and holding Christ forth in God, so that, made heavenly by comparison with the heavenly, we spiritual ones may be made like the spiritual; whose work is nothing else than that they praise the glory of God with a divine voice, as John says: "I saw and heard the voice of many around the throne, and of the living creatures, and of the elders; and their number was ten times a hundred thousand, saying with a loud voice: Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power, and strength, and riches, and patience, and honour, and might, and glory, and blessing. And every creature which is in heaven, and on earth, and the sea, and all things that are in them" (Apoc. v, 11-13). And again he reminds us: "The angels stood around the throne, and the elders, and the four living creatures; and they fell down before the throne on their faces, and worshipped God, saying: Blessing, and glory, and wisdom, and thanksgiving, and honour, and power, and strength be to our God for ever and ever. Amen" (Ibid. vii, 11, 12). HERE ENDS THE SERMON OF SAINT AMBROSE.
